Audit only 
Framework coverage is uneven. Input interception, tool-call request/result, and agent response are close 
to universal across major SDKs. Memory read/write, knowledge retrieval, sub-agent lifecycle, and context-
compaction hooks remain sparse and inconsistent; no framework yet exposes a hook on the skill lifecycle (a 
skill load is caught today only because it runs as a tool call). Assess which events your framework can 
intercept, identify the gaps, and prioritize closing them.

--- page 53 ---
Page 53 
 
genai.owasp.org 
 
GenAI Security Project - Securing Agentic Applications V2 
 
Where to start 
If you wire only two hooks, wire toolCallRequest and agentResponse. 
• toolCallRequest closes the gap between "agent decides to call a tool" and "tool executes" - the gap 
exploited by data-exfiltration injection attacks, and the place to inspect model-generated 
arguments for directory-traversal sequences and unvalidated symlinks before they reach a high-
privilege write. 
• agentResponse covers the next-highest-damage failure mode: unfiltered sensitive data reaching 
the user. 
• memoryStore is next, because cross-session poisoning depends on writing tainted content to 
persistent memory without review. Where a framework does not expose it, reach the same 
protection by screening tainted content where it enters (tool results, retrieved content, user input) 
and at any memory write that runs through a tool call. 
These first two are the ones that are near-universally available. Specify per-call vs. per-batch semantics for 
toolCallRequest, and streaming-disposition semantics for agentResponse. 
Make hooks a hard boundary 
A prompt-layer guardrail ("do not call this tool without approval") is a soft boundary the model can ignore 
under adversarial pressure. A code-layer hook can be a hard boundary, but placement alone does not make it 
one. A hook is a hard boundary only when two conditions hold: 
1. Coverage - it sits on every path to a consequential action. Coverage is the condition that fails quietly: a 
path can reach a consequential action without passing through any hook. During design and testing, 
enumerate the sensitive leverage points and confirm each sits behind a hook. Paths that most often 
escape coverage: direct LLM or tool API calls made outside the harness; sub-agents launched in 
separate processes; MCP servers that call downstream services; tool-initiated callbacks; browser or 
code-execution environments; background jobs; external plugins that write to memory; and streaming 
output released before the response is inspected. For paths that run outside the harness entirely (a sub-
agent in its own process, an MCP server calling downstream), no in-harness hook can reach them - fall 
back to controls that don't rely on the model's cooperation: credential scoping, network-egress controls, 
sandboxing, and server-side authorization (see Section 9). 
2. Resistance to manipulation - the decision at the hook cannot be subverted through the channel it 
polices. A deterministic rule cannot be argued with; a trained classifier scores the input rather than 
following it; an LLM-as-judge is only as strong as its criteria are tight. Where the decision is manipulable, 
the action behind it needs a firmer control as well. 
Make the hook surface explicit: a harness that enumerates the hook points it implements (and, by omission, 
the ones it does not) turns a silent gap into a declared one. Treat the set of implemented hooks as part of the 
harness's interface, not an implementation detail.

--- page 54 ---
Page 54 
 
genai.owasp.org 
 
GenAI Security Project - Securing Agentic Applications V2 
 
Observe-only frameworks. Where native hooks are observe-only (e.g., LangChain, LlamaIndex), you 
cannot enforce a true fail-closed posture through the framework's callback event bus. Hard-code 
enforcement into synchronous wrapper classes around the underlying tool utilities or model clients 
rather than relying on the native listener surface. 
Build it in, and log it 
Hooks are an architectural decision, not a feature to bolt on later - the work is the same whether done calmly 
during initial development or urgently after an incident. Even if early policy is allow-all-with-logging, the hook 
points themselves should be in place from the first version. Map the work across the lifecycle: Design - 
define trust boundaries and the hook points each requires; Implementation - wire hooks into the harness 
execution loop; Testing - exercise critical disposition paths; Pre-release review - verify no sensitive action 
path bypasses a hook; Deployment readiness - confirm hook logs carry policy version, hook version, action 
metadata, and disposition reason codes. 
Every hook invocation should emit a structured log entry (hook point, action intercepted, disposition 
returned, timestamp) - this produces the audit trail the logging section (3.3.3) requires and falls out of the 
architecture rather than needing separate instrumentation. 
How sibling controls map to hooks 
This section is the enforcement layer for controls defined elsewhere: 
• MCP hardening (6.4.2–6.4.4): hash-pin verification, description-poisoning scan, and rug-pull 
revalidation fire at toolCallRequest. 
• Skill hardening (6.4.6): signing, sandboxing, and permission-manifest controls fire at skillRegister / 
skillLoad; the digest pinned at skillRegister is what skillLoad verifies against. 
• Runtime guardrails (3.3.2): input filtering at userMessage, output filtering at agentResponse. 
• HITL (3.1.5): approval gates use the Escalate disposition at toolCallRequest. 
• Memory integrity (3.1.6): read/write controls fire at memoryContextRetrieval and memoryStore. 
• Circuit breakers (3.3.8): emergency halt uses Deny at whichever hook detects the anomaly. 
• Logging & monitoring (3.3.3): structured trace data emits at every hook regardless of disposition. 
• Turn-scoped policies: cumulative-taint tracking and per-turn rate limits enforce at turnStart / 
turnEnd. 
See Section 9 for hooks as runtime enforcement points.

--- page 55 ---
Page 55 
 
genai.owasp.org 
 
GenAI Security Project - Securing Agentic Applications V2 
 
3.3.8 Behavioral Circuit Breakers / Kill Switches 
Detection without an automated response at agent speed is "just expensive logging." A behavioral circuit 
breaker is a real-time, in-line runtime policy engine that can interrupt a misaligned agent faster than a 
human could. It is not a binary on/off switch; it operates in graduated tiers (warn → limit → suspend → kill) 
and can act on an individual sub-agent or the whole system, notifying external agents/tools/MCP servers in 
use. Management can be centralized for coherence while enforcement stays decentralized for speed. 
Specify each circuit breaker against a concrete schema: 
• Policy: the governing rule, baselined through behavioral testing / red-teaming before it is allowed 
to enforce (firewall-style), with support for manual exceptions and tuning. The policy must be 
hardened against tampering by the agentic system(s). 
• Signal: what is monitored - e.g., output-guardrail violations, drift from the declared task goal, 
unexpected sub-agent spawning or loops, plan deviation, non-authoritative memory reads, 
anomalous tool-invocation patterns (fragmentation, ordering, sensitive domain/data 
combinations), tool schema/signature changes, privilege escalation, or system-file ops. 
• Trigger: the condition that fires - e.g., a file write during an information-gathering phase, agent 
self-modification (acquiring new tools or changing its own config), reads of system directories 
when only project files were expected, or any tool schema/signature change. 
• Action: the response - automatic tool revocation above an anomaly threshold, agent quarantine 
(retain observability while blocking external actions), halting the orchestrator, falling back to a safe 
read-only mode, or reducing the agent's action space rather than only stopping it. 
• Rollback: use transaction boundaries, idempotency, and rollback where possible so an interruption 
can be undone; unsafe outcomes trigger containment plus rollback. 
• Audit / incident snapshot: before a kill or rollback, capture a snapshot - freeze the context window 
and preserve the tamper-evident provenance chain (principals, decisions, tools, data accessed) so 
the audit log is a verifiable record rather than a trust assertion. 
Per-component detection & action matrix. The signals and responses differ by where in the architecture 
the circuit breaker sits. Slice detection across the standard key components (KC1–KC6 from Section 2.1):

Worked trigger examples: 
• If a protected task is in an information-gathering stage, a file read is expected, but a file write 
should trigger. 
• If an agent write action is a self-modification (new tools or a change to the agent configuration) it 
should generally trigger - and the trajectory should be considered rogue, not merely blocked. Even 
where self-modification is accepted, the tool-mounting arguments must still be analyzed critically, 
as they may compromise the agent. 
• If a protected task is expected to read business project files, then reading files in system 
directories should trigger.

--- page 57 ---
Page 57 
 
genai.owasp.org 
 
GenAI Security Project - Securing Agentic Applications V2 
 
• If recent history for a group of agents (sub-agents, or agents initiated by the same principal) shows 
a large rate of data-asset deletions (by quantity or size), the cross-agent pattern should trigger. 
• If a sub-agent takes an action that increases access for a principal (e.g., approving an IT ticket 
granting HR-system access), a critical behavior to interrupt could be a second sub-agent updating 
that principal's email address to an external domain. 
• If an LLM judge or graph-based anomaly detector finds an agent action attempting anomalous 
object mutations beyond the intended scope, trigger. A change to a tool schema/signature 
parameters must be blocked or inspected as suspect. 
Common failure modes to design against: high-impact actions misclassified as low-risk; approval logic 
bypassed via an alternate workflow path; agents retrying failed actions and amplifying harm; irreversible 
actions with no rollback; and monitoring that only detects issues after the damage is done.

Page 58 
 
genai.owasp.org 
 
GenAI Security Project - Securing Agentic Applications V2 
 
4. Enhanced Security Actions for 
Agentic AI Systems 
 
Scope of this section. Generic controls that apply to every agentic system - authentication, 
authorization, data protection, code security, monitoring, logging, and prompt security - are the 
lifecycle backbone and live in Section 3. This section focuses on what differs by architecture: the 
deltas for single-agent, central-orchestrator, and swarm systems (orchestrator trust boundaries, 
inter-agent authentication, and swarm peer-to-peer communication). The single-agent baseline 
below (4.1) is retained from V1 as a reference checklist, but where it overlaps with Section 3 the 
Section 3 guidance is authoritative. 
 
4.1 Single-Agent Systems 
4.1.1 Authentication & Authorization 
• Implement OAuth 2.0/OIDC 
o Use authorization code flow with PKCE for enhanced security 
▪ Use when a user is interacting with an agent/LLM through a native app or "one-
page" web interface to prevent client secret leakage or token extraction. 
▪ Use when an agent is acting as a client to a web server without the possibility of a 
client secret. 
o Require explicit user consent through a consent screen showing specific permissions 
requested 
o Resource: Auth0 OAuth 2.0 Implementation Guide 
• Use managed identity services 
o Configure cloud providers' identity services instead of embedding credentials 
o Use AWS IAM roles or Azure Managed Identities to avoid storing secrets 
o Resource (example): AWS IAM Roles for Amazon EC2 
• Apply Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) 
o Define granular roles specific to agent functions, for example, only allow certain roles (user, 
dev, admin) to read/write system memory, etc. 
o Implement permission matrices to track role capabilities 
o Resource: NIST RBAC Standards 
• Grant only minimum necessary permissions 
o Provide agents with only the permissions required for their specific tasks 
o Regularly audit and review permission assignments

--- page 59 ---
Page 59 
 
genai.owasp.org 
 
GenAI Security Project - Securing Agentic Applications V2 
 
• Distinguish between read and write access 
o Separate read and write permissions to minimize risk 
o Default to read-only access and explicitly grant write permissions only when needed 
o Resource: AWS IAM Policy Best Practices 
• Consider just-in-time credential issuance 
o Implement temporary credentials with limited scope and lifetime 
o For managing cross-domain authentication, apply the Token Vault pattern described in 
Section 3.1.8. 
o Credentials only when needed and ensure they expire quickly 
o Resource: HashiCorp Vault Secrets Management 
4.1.2 Data Protection 
• Encrypt sensitive data 
o Use strong encryption algorithms for data at rest and in transit 
o Implement TLS 1.2+ for transit, AES-256-GCM for storage 
o Resource: NIST Cryptographic Standards 
• Implement Data Loss Prevention (DLP) 
o Deploy DLP solutions to monitor and prevent leakage of sensitive information 
o Set up scanning of data inputs/outputs to detect PII, credentials, or other sensitive data 
o Resource: Open Source DLP Solution - OpenDLP 
• Use data classification and sensitivity labels 
o Apply labels that guide AI agent's access and handling of data 
o Data is accessed deterministically and then compared to what kind of data access level the 
agent has. 
▪ §  For example HIPAA data cannot be accessed by a non HIPAA-compliant agent 
o Create tiered classifications like public, internal, confidential, and restricted 
o Resource: Microsoft Information Protection 
• Apply data minimization principles 
o Collect and process only the data necessary for the specific task 
o Create data flow diagrams to identify unnecessary data collection 
o Resource: GDPR Data Minimization Principle 
4.1.3 Code Security 
• Establish automated testing pipelines 
o Set up CI/CD pipelines with integrated security scanning 
o Include SAST, DAST, and SCA tools in the pipeline 
o Resource: OWASP DevSecOps Guideline 
• Conduct thorough code reviews

--- page 60 ---
Page 60 
 
genai.owasp.org 
 
GenAI Security Project - Securing Agentic Applications V2 
 
o Implement both automated and manual code reviews before deployment 
o Use checklists specific to AI system security concerns 
o Resource: OWASP Code Review Guide 
• Monitor dependencies 
o Continuously check external libraries for vulnerabilities 
o Set up automated dependency scanning and alerts 
o Resource: GitHub Dependabot 
4.1.4 Monitoring & Incident Response 
• Log all actions and establish baselines 
o Record comprehensive logs of all agent activities 
o Establish behavioral patterns to detect anomalies 
o Maintain a log chain of thought for particularly sensitive operations. These logs should be 
assigned the same data classification as the highest level of data involved in their 
generation. 
o Resource: Cloud Security Alliance - Security Logging Guidelines 
• Implement real-time anomaly detection 
o Use machine learning to detect unusual behavior patterns (using an ML enabled SIEM tool) 
o Deploy systems that can identify deviations from normal operation 
o Resource: Awesome Anomaly Detection 
• Set up alerts for suspicious events 
o Configure notifications for unusual patterns or security concerns 
o Alert on access attempts to sensitive endpoints, spikes in requests, unusual IP origins 
o Resource: PagerDuty Incident Response Documentation 
• Develop incident response plans 
o Create detailed procedures for addressing security breaches 
o Include containment, investigation, remediation, and recovery steps 
o Resource: NIST Computer Security Incident Handling Guide 
• Build emergency off-switches 
o Implement kill switches to immediately revoke access privileges 
o Create automated and manual mechanisms to stop agent operations 
o Resource: Anthropic AI Safety Research 
4.1.5 Prompt Security 
• Implement input validation 
o Filter user inputs using rule-based patterns and NLP techniques or filtering for multi-modal 
processing 
o Check for malicious patterns before processing by the AI system (WAF Rules)

--- page 61 ---
Page 61 
 
genai.owasp.org 
 
GenAI Security Project - Securing Agentic Applications V2 
 
o Resource: Guide to LLM Prompt Injection Defenses 
• Apply content filtering on AI outputs 
o Screen AI-generated responses for inappropriate or harmful content 
o Use both pattern matching and ML-based content classifiers 
o Resource: Perspective API for Content Moderation 
• Harden system prompts 
o Embed security policies directly into the AI's foundational instructions 
o Structure prompts to reject harmful requests and maintain guardrails 
o Resource: OpenAI System Message Guidelines 
• Sanitize all inputs 
o Clean and normalize inputs to prevent injection attacks 
o Remove or escape special characters and formatting that could alter behavior 
o Resource: OWASP Input Validation Cheat Sheet 
4.2 Multi-Agent Systems with Central Orchestrator 
Multi Agent: Multiple intelligent agents that interact with each other and a shared environment to solve 
problems or achieve goals. The agents can operate independently, discern their surroundings, make 
decisions, and act. The central orchestrator is responsible for coordinating the agents' interactions, 
assigning tasks, and maintaining the overall workflow or state. 
4.2.1 Authentication & Authorization 
• Use authentication and authorization controls from 4.1.1 
• Establish separation of control planes 
o Create clear separation between different agent functionalities 
o Utilize the user assumption architecture pattern from section 2.2.1 to enforce user 
permissions on an agent 
o Maintain distinct permission sets for each agent based on least privilege 
o Resource: AWS Separation of Control and Data Planes 
• Authenticate and verify all agent interactions (see section 4.2.3) 
• Restrict discovery to known and trusted servers 
o Hard code discovery servers in agent instructions 
o Prevent agents from communicating with discovery servers using network and logical 
controls 
4.2.2 Orchestrator Security 
• Harden the central orchestrator's API 
o Implement robust authentication and authorization mechanisms 
o Use rate limiting, input validation, and detailed logging

--- page 62 ---
Page 62 
 
genai.owasp.org 
 
GenAI Security Project - Securing Agentic Applications V2 
 
o Resource: OWASP API Security Top 10 
• Protect against control-flow hijacking 
o Validate agent responses to prevent manipulation of the orchestrator's decisions 
o Implement integrity checks on operational metadata and agent outputs 
o Resource: MITRE ATLAS Framework for AI Threats 
• Mitigate the "confused deputy problem" 
o Prevent scenarios where trusted components are tricked into performing unauthorized 
actions 
o Implement additional context validation and cross-check requests 
o Resource: The Confused Deputy Problem 
• Formalize On-Behalf-Of (OBO) delegation and intent binding 
o Delegate user authority via OAuth 2.0 Token Exchange (RFC 8693), never raw user 
credentials. Issue short-lived, task-bound, audience-bound tokens; each sub-agent or 
intermediary performs its own exchange. 
o Enforce delegation depth limits and monotonic scope attenuation: each hop's token is a 
proper subset of its parent's, with decaying TTL and cascade revocation. 
o Bind authorization to the declared user intent for the current task, and deny actions outside 
that intent even when permission and capability would otherwise allow them. Have the 
orchestrator pass a signed, immutable, intent-locked task descriptor that sub-agents 
cannot rewrite mid-chain. This is the structural mitigation for the confused deputy problem. 
o For MCP/OAuth proxy architectures, avoid static client IDs (vulnerable to consent-cookie 
reuse via dynamically registered malicious clients): use per-client consent storage and an 
MCP-level consent UI with CSRF protection, and prohibit token passthrough.

--- page 63 ---
Page 63 
 
genai.owasp.org 
 
GenAI Security Project - Securing Agentic Applications V2 
 
 
Figure 4.1: On-Behalf-Of delegation from the user through the orchestrator to each sub-agent. Every hop 
performs its own OAuth 2.0 Token Exchange and receives a short-lived, task-bound, audience-bound token 
whose scope is a proper subset of its parent's, with decaying TTL, cascade revocation and a delegation 
depth limit. The signed, immutable, intent-locked task descriptor travels with the chain unchanged. The 
narrowing is enforced by authorization server policy at each exchange. 
4.2.3 Inter-Agent Communication 
• Implement secure communication protocols 
o Use protocols with strong encryption for all agent interactions 
o Implement mutual TLS (mTLS) for two-way authentication 
o Resource: Mutual TLS (mTLS) Authentication 
• Verify the identity of each communicating agent 
o Use certificate-based or token-based authentication mechanisms 
o Resource: JWT Authentication Best Practices 
• Use secure message queuing systems 
o Implement message brokers with security features for asynchronous communication 
o Use systems like RabbitMQ, Kafka, or NATS with authentication and encryption 
o Resource: RabbitMQ Security 
• Deploy Policy Enforcement Points (PEPs) 
o Add security checkpoints to communication channels for policy enforcement

--- page 64 ---
Page 64 
 
genai.owasp.org 
 
GenAI Security Project - Securing Agentic Applications V2 
 
o Implement as middleware or service proxies that validate each interaction 
• Apply rate limiting for agent interactions 
o Prevent abuse by limiting the frequency of requests between agents 
o Implement exponential backoff for failed requests 
o Resource: GitHub API Rate Limiting 
4.2.4 Trust Boundaries 
• Apply Zero Trust security principles 
o Implement "never trust, always verify" approach across the architecture 
o Verify every access request regardless of source 
o Resource: NIST SP 800-207 Zero Trust Architecture 
• Implement network segmentation and agent isolation 
o Create distinct security zones within the system 
o Limit interconnectedness of agents to contain potential breaches 
o Resource: NSA Network Segmentation Guide 
• Use containerization technologies 
o Sandbox individual agents using Docker or similar technologies 
o Restrict access to underlying OS and system resources 
o Resource: Docker Security Best Practices 
 
4.3 Multi-Agent Systems with Swarm Architecture 
4.3.1 Authentication & Authorization 
• Use authentication and authorization controls from 4.1.1 and 4.2.1 
• Identify trusted agents and actions 
o Swarm systems don't necessarily have an easy guide post for the correct action and trusted 
collaborators. Assign this trust and action outside the agentic flow 
o Limit or prevent the swarm from adding new agents without human guidance. 
4.3.2 Decentralized Identity & Trust 
• Implement Decentralized Identifiers (DIDs) 
o Use W3C standard DIDs for self-sovereign agent identities 
o Enable verification without central authority 
o Resource: W3C Decentralized Identifiers Specification 
• Use Verifiable Credentials (VCs) 
o Implement VCs for agents to prove specific attributes 
o Enable secure and verifiable proofs of capabilities or authorizations

--- page 65 ---
Page 65 
 
genai.owasp.org 
 
GenAI Security Project - Securing Agentic Applications V2 
 
o Resource: W3C Verifiable Credentials Data Model 
• Create decentralized reputation systems 
o Build systems where agents develop reputation scores based on behavior 
o Use these scores to make trust decisions for collaboration 
o Resource: The OpenCerts Framework for Verifiable Claims 
• Guard against Sybil-inflated reputation 
o Cheap-to-mint identities can mutually vouch to inflate a malicious agent's score faster than 
genuine behavior would earn it 
o Pair reputation with a minting-cost control: staking, human-sponsored first credential, or 
rate-limited DID registration  
How? 
• Agent Identity: Each AI agent can have its own DID, providing a persistent, verifiable identity 
across different interactions and environments. 
• Credential-Based Trust: Verifiable Credentials can establish an agent's capabilities, permissions, 
or trust level within the system. 
• Inter-Agent Authentication: Agents can verify each other's identities and credentials without 
centralized coordination. 
• Provenance Tracking: DIDs can help track the origin of information or actions in a multi-agent 
system, establishing clear provenance. 
• Access Control: VCs can determine which agents have access to specific resources or capabilities 
within the system. 
• Role Specialization: Credentials can formalize specialized roles among different agents (e.g., 
reasoning agent, retrieval agent, etc.). 
4.3.3 Secure Peer-to-Peer Communication 
• Select appropriate P2P protocols 
o Choose protocols based on specific security and performance needs 
o Consider TLS/SSL, DTLS, Noise Protocol, or specialized frameworks 
o Resource: Noise Protocol Framework Specification 
• Ensure both encryption and authentication 
o Implement strong encryption to protect confidentiality 
o Use robust authentication to verify identity of participating agents 
o Resource: NIST SP 800-175B: Guideline for Using Cryptographic Standards

--- page 66 ---
Page 66 
 
genai.owasp.org 
 
GenAI Security Project - Securing Agentic Applications V2 
 
4.4 Cross-Architecture Security Considerations 
• Secure API Design for Agent Communication 
o Implement standardized interfaces with comprehensive input validation. (See Appendix E 
for protocols/standards) 
o Apply rate limiting and authentication regardless of architecture 
o Resource: OWASP API Security Top 10 
• Continuous Security Testing 
o Regularly scan all agent architectures for vulnerabilities 
o Implement automated and manual security testing processes 
o Resource: NIST Security Testing Guidelines 
• Security Monitoring and Threat Detection 
o Implement comprehensive monitoring regardless of architecture 
o Adjust detection strategies based on architectural specifics 
o Resource: MITRE ATT&CK Framework 
• Secure Agent Updates and Maintenance 
o Implement secure update mechanisms for all architectures 
o Verify integrity of updates before deployment 
o Resource: NIST Secure Software Development Framework 
This comprehensive list provides developers with practical security actions covering all major aspects of 
agentic AI system security across different architectures, along with relevant web resources for further 
reading.

5. Key Operational 
Capabilities 
 
Connecting Agentic AI applications with other systems or environments such as APIs, databases, code 
interpreters, web browsers, or the operating system enables great functionality (skills). However, each new 
operational connection poses unique security concerns, ranging from data breaches and illegal actions to 
system compromise. The following listed controls are necessary to reduce these inherent risks. 
5.0 Capability Control Matrix 
Before the per-capability controls below, classify each operational capability the agent holds along the 
dimensions in the matrix. This makes the capability-composition gate from 2.7.3 (Lethal Trifecta / Rule of 
Two) concrete: if a single agent's capabilities together cover untrusted input + sensitive data + external 
communication, the design must add sandboxing, HITL, runtime monitoring, or architectural separation - or 
remove one leg.

For each capability also record the required telemetry (what must be logged) and an escalation trigger (the 
condition that forces HITL, throttling, or a circuit-breaker action - see 3.3.8). 
• Trigger: A declared effect annotation moving in the permissive direction (e.g., destructiveHint 
changing from true to false). 
• Binding Requirement: When a gate consumes an effect annotation, bind the declaration to the 
contract it was declared against. Treat an absent annotation as unobserved rather than safe.

5.1 KC6.1 – API Access 
Core Threats: Unauthorized data access/leakage (T3), API abuse (DoS, cost overruns) (T4, T2), Compromised 
keys (T3, T9) 
Controls: 
1. Enforce Least Privilege with Fine-Grained OAuth Scopes or Limited API Keys 
• Define the minimum necessary activities for task completion (e.g. never grant an admin's complete 
access to an agent) 
• Grant access solely to essential assets with minimal access scope / issue access tokens only to 
necessary clients/agents 
• Implementation Options: 
o OAuth 2.0: Establish specific OAuth scopes using services like: Okta, Auth0, Keycloak, 
Cloud provider integrated services 
o SDKs: Utilize Authlib or Passport.js to streamline OAuth operations 
o API Keys: Employ provider features to enforce limits: 
▪ AWS API Gateway allows restriction to specific API stages/methods 
▪ Configure IP address restrictions or read-only access where available 
o Cloud IAM: For agents operating as cloud services (e.g., AWS Lambda, Google Cloud 
Functions), assign specific IAM roles with restricted permissions 
2. Set up Allow/Deny Lists for APIs 
• Prevent manipulation via prompt injection or compromised tools 
• Clearly define authorized domains or URL pathways 
• Implementation Approaches: 
o Configure a list of permitted base URLs (Allow-List) or URL patterns 
o Authenticate target URLs against this list before executing external requests 
o Use outward proxy or API Gateway to permit connections only to pre-approved destinations 
o For containerized agents, implement network policies to limit outgoing traffic 
3. Prefer API Templates Over Complete LLM-Generated API Calls 
• Mitigate risks of unsafe or malformed API calls 
• Improve reliability by hard coding unchanging/common fields 
4. Best Practices: 
• Use prepared templates where LLMs only populate established parameters 
• Utilize templating libraries like Jinja2 
• Leverage structured output capabilities with strictly defined schemas 
• Define parameter types and requirements before sending requests

--- page 70 ---
Page 70 
 
genai.owasp.org 
 
GenAI Security Project - Securing Agentic Applications V2 
 
• Sanitize web-fetched content using tools like DOMPurify 
• Implement Content Security Policy (CSP) when rendering content 
 
5.2 KC6.2 – Code Execution 
Core Threats: Arbitrary code execution (RCE) (T11, T3), Code injection (T11, T2), DoS via resource exhaustion 
(T4), Leakage of confidential information (T6) 
Controls: 
1. Implement Mandatory Sandboxing 
• OS-level isolation, containers, VMs, WebAssembly, or cloud solutions 
• Reference implementations: 
o NVIDIA's WebAssembly Sandboxing 
o LangChain's E2B Data Analysis 
2. Perform Static Analysis on Agent-Generated Code 
• Use tools like: 
o Bandit for Python 
o Semgrep for multi-language analysis 
o CodeShield for LLM-generated code 
3. Enforce Resource Limitations 
• Set strict CPU, memory, and execution time limits 
• Implement timeouts for all operations 
4. Additional Security Measures 
• Use code signing or verification when possible 
• Implement strict file system and network restrictions 
• Use allow-lists for permitted commands 
• Require Human-In-The-Loop (HITL) approval for high-risk operations 
• Sanitize all executed code output 
• Implement runtime monitoring during execution

--- page 71 ---
Page 71 
 
genai.owasp.org 
 
GenAI Security Project - Securing Agentic Applications V2 
 
5.3 KC6.3 – Database Execution (Queries and RAG access) 
Core Threats: SQL injection (T2), Unauthorized data exposure/modification (T3), RAG data 
poisoning/sensitive data retrieval (T1, T5, T3) 
Controls: 
1. Use Managed Vector Databases with Access Controls 
• Restrict data ingest to match the access control capability (never ingest data that can't be 
protected from unauthorized users) 
• Apply data classification labels to enforce user privilege 
o Utilize specialized RBAC RAGs like Elastic RAG 
o Pinecone with authentication platforms like Clerk 
o Authorization platforms like Aserto 
2. Implement Query Safety Measures 
• Use parameterized or template queries/ORMs exclusively. Never construct SQL using string 
concatenation. 
• Grant database access via least-privilege user accounts, e.g. SELECT only, limited tables, or 
row/column level security 
• Filter/block dangerous SQL keywords (e.g., DROP, TRUNCATE) 
• Validate all user inputs influencing queries - if possible, derive from controlled channels only vs 
context window. 
3. RAG-Specific Controls 
• Implement post-retrieval filtering to check for sensitive content (PII) before agent use 
• Apply content verification before embedding into vector stores 
• Rate-limit retrieval operations 
4. Limitation (Excessive Retrieval)

--- page 72 ---
Page 72 
 
genai.owasp.org 
 
GenAI Security Project - Securing Agentic Applications V2 
 
5.4 KC6.4 – Web Use 
Core Threats: Malicious web content (XSS, exploits) (T11), Leakage of confidential information (T6), 
Phishing/deception (T7), Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) (T2, T3), Access to user's browser data - 
Sensitive Data Exposure (T3) 
Controls: 
1. Sandbox Browser Components 
• Run in tightly controlled environments 
• Avoid using extensions or operating directly in the user's browser 
2. Implement URL Security 
• Use URL filtering with allow lists 
• Leverage Secure Web Gateway (SWG) or Data Loss Prevention (DLP) 
• Perform reputation checks on target domains 
• Enforce proper TLS verification 
• Detect and block open redirects or excessive redirection chains. Further, use DNS-based filtering 
in addition to HTTP-level filtering. 
3. Apply Protective Measures 
• Use network segmentation to prevent access to internal systems (mitigating SSRF) 
• Throttle web access rate to prevent abuse 
• Restrict downloadable file types 
• Implement content sanitization before processing 
• Inspect embedded/linked content (e.g., iframes, JS-injected sources) 
4. Logging and Monitoring 
• Log all URL accesses and HTTP responses

--- page 73 ---
Page 73 
 
genai.owasp.org 
 
GenAI Security Project - Securing Agentic Applications V2 
 
5.5 KC6.5 – Controlling PC Operations (Filesystem, OS 
Commands) 
Core Threats: Unauthorized file access/modification (T3), Arbitrary OS command execution (T11, T3, T2), 
Lateral movement (T3) 
Controls: 
1. Apply Strict Isolation 
• Use OS-level sandboxing 
• Run agents as restricted users with minimal privileges 
• Consider dedicated containers or VMs for isolation 
2. Implement Access Controls 
• Define strict allow/deny lists for permitted OS operations and file paths 
• Use virtual filesystem interfaces where appropriate 
• Intercept OS command calls to enforce allow-lists 
3. Limit accumulation of sensitive data 
• To maintain its status, sandbox should not accumulate data and sessions 
4. Enhance Monitoring and Oversight 
• Log all OS-level actions performed by the agent 
• Consider HITL approval for critical operations 
• Implement command validation before execution 
5.5.1 Coding & Computer-Use Agent Guardrails 
Coding agents and "computer use" agents are, by definition, a Lethal Trifecta (see 2.7.3): they process 
untrusted input (repositories, issues, web pages, screens), hold access to sensitive data (credentials, 
source, git, CI/CD, authenticated sessions), and can communicate externally. They therefore require the 
controls below in addition to the general KC6.5 controls. 
• Treat repository-level configuration as an untrusted, execution-layer supply-chain vector. Files 
such as CLAUDE.md, .cursorrules, .github/copilot-instructions.md, mcp.json, and .cursorignore 
travel inside cloned/forked/shared repos and can control agent behavior (system prompts, allowed 
tools, MCP connections) before any trust dialog. Documented cases include a repo settings file 
redirecting the model API endpoint to an attacker (capturing requests/credentials) and a changed 
.cursorignore exposing credential files. Treat user-level config as trusted and repo-level config as 
untrusted; require a user approval gate before repo-provided instructions or repo-controlled config 
can execute; and integrity-check MCP server configs.

--- page 74 ---
Page 74 
 
genai.owasp.org 
 
GenAI Security Project - Securing Agentic Applications V2 
 
• Command permission model: default-deny plus an allowlist. Make allow/deny lists for commands, 
file paths, and network operator-configurable (not only developer-set). Validate that a command is 
grounded in session intent before running it, and escalate to HITL rather than blanket-blocking the 
session. Use risk-based HITL to avoid approval fatigue. 
• Restricted git / destructive-operation safety: prevent destructive operations (e.g., force push, 
reset --hard, DROP TABLE), protect branch policies, and require commit signing. 
• Path & credential hygiene: use .ignore-style configs to keep credentials out of context and long-
term memory; detect "toxic combinations" (sensitive-file access plus an external tool call in one 
session); validate arguments for directory traversal and symlinks before high-privilege writes. 
• Repo isolation / sandboxing: clone, read, and modify repositories inside an OS- or cloud-VM-
isolated sandbox (kernel-isolated filesystem and execution, restricted inbound/outbound network); 
make tools "sandbox-aware"; define sub-agent / worktree permission-inheritance rules. 
• Session isolation for browser/computer use: use dedicated browser profiles rather than the 
user's authenticated sessions, and redact screenshots / sensitive on-screen output. 
• Dry-run / preview risky operations before committing them, and intercept agent-to-LLM and 
agent-to-tool I/O (via hooks, see 3.3.7) to scan for jailbreaks, sensitive data, malicious code/URLs, 
and drift between an action and prior intent.

--- page 75 ---
Page 75 
 
genai.owasp.org 
 
GenAI Security Project - Securing Agentic Applications V2 
 
5.6 KC6.6 – Operating Critical Systems (e.g., SCADA controls) 
Core Threats: Catastrophic physical outcomes (T2, T3, T6, T7), Malicious control injection (T2, T6), False data 
influencing decisions (T1, T5) 
Controls: 
1. Apply Maximum Isolation 
• Use air-gapped or highly segmented networks 
• Implement physical security measures 
2. Enforce Multi-Factor Authentication 
• Switch to external flow to Require MFA for specific sensitive actions where possible - do not use 
agent to mediate MFA flow or retain privileged session 
• Implement mandatory HITL for every critical action, succinct and engaging enough to retain the 
user's attention each time (excessive/inefficient prompting results in indiscriminate approval) 
3. Implement Safety Mechanisms 
• Default agent permissions to read-only monitoring 
• Use anomaly detection tuned to system safety parameters 
• Adhere to industrial control security standards 
• Ensure physical interlocks and emergency overrides exist

Page 76 
 
genai.owasp.org 
 
GenAI Security Project - Securing Agentic Applications V2 
 
6. Agentic AI and the Supply 
Chain 
 
6.1 Code Security 
6.1.1 - Third party libraries & frameworks 
• Standard supply chain applies 
• SCA scanning 
• Hashes & package locks for 3rd party versioning 
• SBOMs 
• Licenses & provenance should be validated for third party libraries before install 
6.1.2 - LLM/Agent generated code 
• Utilize sandboxing for any agent generated/run code (3.2.3) 
• Validate packages before running generated code 
• HITL for high-risk code execution operations 
 
6.2 Environments & Development 
6.2.1 - LLM / Logic System 
• Use the same LLMs in lower environments & production for higher reliability 
• Ensure the provenance of LLMs in a public registry (like Hugging Face) by verifying hashes and 
contributors 
• Use LLM and SCA scanners to scan for both third-party package vulnerabilities and security issues 
within LLM code (where applicable) 
6.2.2 - Version Control & Code Management 
• Utilize version control with LLMs & logic systems to track behavior 
• Implement version control on prompts & instructions to increase reliability and auditability of 
behavior 
• Use commit IDs and hashes for data changes

--- page 77 ---
Page 77 
 
genai.owasp.org 
 
GenAI Security Project - Securing Agentic Applications V2 
 
6.2.3 - Permission management 
• Don't give agents access to the repositories/data sources which build/deploy them 
• Manage permissions to data sources outside the environments the agent is running in 
• Use code to modify IAM/roles permissions for agents to review changes 
 
6.3 Agent & Tool Discovery 
6.3.1 - Agent Cards 
• Identify trust relationships with agent cards and descriptions, and minimize trust with unvalidated 
agent systems 
• Employ DIDs for agent verification and authentication 
• Apply the tool-definition integrity controls in 6.4.2 to agent cards: pin the card by digest at first 
trust, re-fetch and re-compare on a defined schedule, and treat a changed card as a re-approval 
trigger rather than a silent update. 
6.3.2 - Local vs Remote Agent Registries 
• Use logical or network barrier between local & remote registries to prevent registry confusion and 
accidental agent boundary traversal 
• Classify and separate private and public agents, data and actions. Prevent agents from sharing data 
or performing actions across these boundaries 
• Use trust relationships and controls like certificate pinning to ensure agents only communicate 
with approved registries and environments 
 
6.4 Tool Lifecycle & MCP-Specific Supply-Chain Controls 
This section covers the supply chain for the tools an agent uses - including MCP servers and Agent Skills. The 
goal is actionable build/runtime control, not an AI-BOM or compliance artifact. MCP is treated as a tool-
integration profile of KC5 (see 2.1 note under KC5.3); the controls below are where its hardening 
requirements live. 
6.4.1 Standardized Provenance Record 
To ensure consistency across tool, skill, and memory auditing, all components must implement a unified 
Provenance Record schema. This allows runtime enforcement and monitoring logic to treat trust decisions 
uniformly - for example: 
• source_id: Unique identifier for the origin (e.g., server URI, repository URL).

--- page 78 ---
Page 78 
 
genai.owasp.org 
 
GenAI Security Project - Securing Agentic Applications V2 
 
• author: Verified publisher or entity identity (e.g., DID, signing principal). 
• timestamp: ISO-8601 record of when the artifact was created or captured. 
• trust_level: Categorical classification (e.g., System, Vetted, User, Untrusted). 
• integrity_hash: Cryptographic digest (SHA-256 or better) of the artifact content. 
• last_verified_at: Timestamp of the most recent validation check against the source. 
6.4.2 - Tool onboarding & catalog governance 
• Maintain an internal vetted registry of approved tools / MCP servers; block direct pulls from public 
repositories in production. Tool/server "squatting" and "slopsquatting" (names a model is likely to 
hallucinate or suggest) make open registries an active attack surface. 
• For each server/tool onboarded: SAST-scan its code, produce an SBOM of its dependencies, and 
run it in a behavioral sandbox to verify it performs only its advertised function. Verify publisher 
identity and prefer canonical sources. 
• Require a security-review admission gate before any new tool is added; test tool updates in staging 
before production; actively decommission unused tools. 
• Maintain a signed, version-pinned catalog manifest (server URI, tool name, approval timestamp) 
signed with a key held outside the agent runtime and stored in version control. Each entry must 
adhere to the Standardized Provenance Record (6.4.0). An unsigned or unverifiable manifest is a 
deployment-gate failure. 
6.4.3 - Tool definition integrity (anti "rug-pull") 
• Pin tool descriptions and schemas by cryptographic hash at first registration. Re-hash on every 
session start and on every catalog refresh, and compare against the pinned values; block execution 
when a live definition no longer matches its approved digest. 
• A hash mismatch blocks the tool pending operator re-approval, with an alert that includes the diff. 
Define explicit re-approval triggers: a change to a tool's name, schema, or description; a change to 
the server's TLS certificate; the server hostname resolving to a new address; or a changed tool list. 
• Never carry "approved" status across session boundaries ("approve once, trust forever" is the 
vulnerability). Apply a maximum Approval TTL; expiry triggers automatic re-validation, not silent 
re-approval. Record, alongside every pinned digest, the observation timestamp and the age of the 
source snapshot at the time of approval. An approval is only as fresh as the input it was computed 
against. Audit staleness arises from two independent producers: subject drift after judgment and 
instrument lag at judgment. Digest pinning models only the first; instrument lag - where the 
evaluation timestamp postdates the last day the judged text was published - emains invisible to 
models assuming the scanner sees the present. 
• Catalog-drift detection: alert when a server adds, removes, renames, or changes tools even if no 
individual approved definition changed, and keep an append-only catalog audit log.

--- page 79 ---
Page 79 
 
genai.owasp.org 
 
GenAI Security Project - Securing Agentic Applications V2 
 
6.4.4 - Treat tool descriptions and responses as adversarial input 
• Scan every tool name, description, and input/output schema for hidden-instruction patterns before 
admitting it to context (Tool Poisoning); reject tools that fail the scan. A pattern baseline includes 
injection delimiters (<IMPORTANT>, IGNORE PREVIOUS), cross-tool-orchestration phrases ("before 
using this tool…"), credential/path references, exfiltration patterns, base64 blobs, and zero-width 
Unicode. Render the full description to the operator at registration, not just the tool name. 
• Enforce strict isolation between tool descriptions: a description must not reference, modify, or 
condition behavior on other tools (Cross-Tool Shadowing). 
• Validate every tool response against the approved schema before it enters the model context; a 
non-conforming response must not enter context. MCP tool responses are a primary indirect-
prompt-injection surface. 
• Pattern/regex sanitization is insufficient as the primary defense (fragmented multi-layer payloads 
evade filters and reassemble at the sink). Prioritize schema enforcement and runtime isolation 
over content sanitization. 
6.4.5 - Asset Access Control Matrix 
To prevent unauthorized data exfiltration and configuration hijacking, access to sensitive security assets 
must be strictly policed. The following matrix defines the authoritative read/write boundaries for 
credentials, configuration files, and identity assets across the tool and skill lifecycle. Any attempt to deviate 
from these boundaries must trigger a behavioral circuit breaker (see 3.3.8).

7. Assuring Agentic 
Applications 
 
Assurance strategies for agentic applications must extend beyond static testing. Consider these 
approaches: 
Scope of this section. This guide's scope excludes red-teaming playbooks; detailed red-team 
methodology, attack recipes, and benchmark-tool catalogs belong to the separate OWASP ASI Red 
Teaming Guide and are referenced rather than reproduced here. The focus of this section is 
lifecycle validation: tying assurance back to the system's intended scope, assumptions, threat 
model, controls, behavioral tests, runtime monitoring, and regression triggers. The red-teaming 
material retained below (7.1) is a brief orientation and pointer to that guide. 
7.0 Assurance as Lifecycle Validation 
This chapter follows the agentic security lifecycle in two halves. The first half is design-time assurance: the 
architectural and configuration choices that bound what an agent can do before it ever runs. The second half 
is validation that the design holds, covered through red teaming (7.1) and behavioral testing (7.2). The 
ordering is deliberate - testing has nothing to falsify until the design has named its own assumptions. 
7.0.1 Assurance objective 
The objective is to determine whether an agentic application is sufficiently constrained, tested, and 
monitored to operate within its intended scope. Assurance does not mean proving an application is perfectly 
safe; it means establishing a risk-based, evidence-backed case that the application's design assumptions 
hold under realistic and adversarial conditions. It applies familiar software-assurance practices to agentic 
systems - requirements traceability, control validation, regression testing, release evidence, change-impact 
analysis, and production monitoring: define what the system is supposed to do, identify what it must not do, 
implement controls, test whether those controls hold, and revalidate the affected parts when behavior-
defining elements change. 
The assurance scope is the actual application being assessed - its purpose, trust boundaries, data flows, 
data access, tools, memory, orchestration, identity model, external integrations, deployment context, and 
operational controls - not a generic agent pattern. This holds whether the application is a simple single-
agent workflow or a complex system with delegation, tool chains, retrieval, long-running state, or external 
protocols.

--- page 82 ---
Page 82 
 
genai.owasp.org 
 
GenAI Security Project - Securing Agentic Applications V2 
 
The chain that traces design intent to runtime evidence: 
design scope → assumptions → threat model → controls → validation tests → runtime monitoring 
→ regression triggers. 
 
Figure 7.1: The assurance chain, design scope, assumptions, threat model, controls, validation tests, 
runtime monitoring and regression triggers, with the loop a trigger sends back to the scope: a partial replay 
of the affected design checks, red team scenarios and behavioral cases, with the scope updated first. An 
undocumented decision to skip revalidation is itself an assurance gap. 
7.0.2 Definitions used in this chapter 
• Intended scope - what the application is for: its purpose, the behavior it should and should not 
exhibit, the data and tools it may use, and the trust boundaries within which these hold. It must be 
precise: a scope stated vaguely ("act as a helpful assistant") cannot be configured, tested, or 
monitored against. For any given action a reviewer must be able to decide whether it falls within the 
boundary - including capability compositions that remain out of scope even where each capability is 
individually permitted (see 2.7.3). 
• Behavior-defining element - any configurable element of the deployed application whose 
modification can change behavior in a way that may invalidate a prior design assumption, control, 
or test result: the model (KC1), the system instructions, the tool/integration set (KC5), the memory

--- page 83 ---
Page 83 
 
genai.owasp.org 
 
GenAI Security Project - Securing Agentic Applications V2 
 
architecture and retrieval sources (KC4), the orchestration and workflow logic (KC2, KC3), the 
permission and identity scopes, and the deployment/environment controls (KC6). A change to any 
of them triggers the partial replay described in 7.0.5. 
• Harness - the collection of behavior-defining elements other than the model (KC1). It determines 
which decision points the model encounters and what context each decision sees; the model's 
outputs in turn determine the harness's next state. The deployed application is the joint product of 
model and harness, which is why the trajectory - not any single decision - is the unit that reflects 
the system as built (7.2.2). 
• Configuration constraint - the specific value assigned to a behavior-defining element at design 
time (which tools are enabled, which memory scope is permitted, which permission boundary is 
set). Intended scope states what the application should do; configuration constraints are how the 
design enforces it. 
Note on evidence (no new KC). The source proposal introduced a "KC7 - Behavioral Observation & Evidence" 
with a behavioral tuple as the atomic unit of observation (a structured record of one agent action capturing 
agent identity, session context, triggering input, reasoning step, action taken, state change, active policy 
context, and timestamp). Per this guide's no-new-KC rule, that is kept as an evidence/observability concept 
rather than a key component: the behavioral tuple is the structured audit record produced by the logging and 
hook instrumentation already specified in 3.3.3 and 3.3.7, and it is the foundation for the custom benchmarks 
in 7.2.1. 
7.0.3 The assurance case 
An application reaches an acceptable assurance state when its intended scope is explicitly defined, its 
design constraints are documented, its main risk paths are understood, its controls are linked to tests that 
can validate or challenge those assumptions, and its known limitations and residual risks are documented 
and accepted by an accountable owner. The assurance case is the combination of: 
• Declared design assumptions - the scope, trust boundaries, capability constraints, and threat 
model the system was designed against; 
• Validation evidence - structured, traceable proof those assumptions were tested under conditions 
that could falsify them; 
• Runtime evidence - continuous, queryable proof that the controls encoding those assumptions 
remain live and correctly operating in production; 
• Change traceability - a record of how the assurance case was updated when the system changed. 
Assurance is the connective layer between the rest of the guide: architecture defines the boundaries, 
developer controls implement them, capability controls constrain high-risk actions, supply-chain controls 
preserve the integrity of behavior-defining artifacts, deployment controls enforce runtime limits, and 
monitoring detects drift. Section 7 asks whether the complete system still behaves within the scope it was

--- page 84 ---
Page 84 
 
genai.owasp.org 
 
GenAI Security Project - Securing Agentic Applications V2 
 
designed to satisfy. This chapter does not prescribe red-teaming playbooks, general model-evaluation 
methods, accuracy benchmarks, compliance mappings, or governance processes. 
7.0.4 Design-time assurance scoping 
Before any testing begins, the design must produce explicit, testable statements of what the system should 
do, what it must not do, and under what conditions those constraints hold - these are the targets red 
teaming and behavioral validation will try to falsify. A complete design-time assurance scope contains: 
• Intended capability boundaries - for each operational capability exposed through KC5 and 
reachable in the operational environment (KC6), state explicitly what the agent is permitted to do 
and what it is not. 
• Trust boundary declarations - for each input source (user prompts, tool results, memory retrievals, 
inter-agent messages, web content), declare the trust level assigned and the controls applied 
before it influences reasoning or action. 
• Threat assumptions - state which ASI T&M threats the design mitigates, which it accepts as 
residual risk, and which are out of scope; this is the reference for red-team prioritization. 
• Safe failure states - for each high-risk capability, define what the agent does when a control fires a 
DENY/ESCALATE, when a tool call fails, or when a plan produces output that cannot be validated. 
• Operational-environment assumptions - state any assumptions about the deployment 
environment that, if violated, would invalidate the controls. 
These statements become the living reference for every assurance activity, versioned alongside the 
codebase. When the system changes, the scope is updated first. 
7.0.5 Design-to-validation handoff and revalidation triggers 
Red teaming and behavioral validation are not independent activities applied after design - they are the 
means by which the design is challenged. The handoff is a contract: 
• Design defines the intended boundary and expected in-scope behavior. 
• Threat modeling identifies how that boundary may fail. 
• Controls are selected to prevent, reduce, detect, or contain those failures. 
• Red teaming attempts to falsify the assumptions behind the controls. 
• Behavioral validation checks the application remains useful within scope - performing authorized 
work reliably without expanding beyond its boundaries or defensively blocking legitimate in-scope 
behavior. 
• Findings are converted into remediation, regression tests, monitoring signals, or design updates. 
If a design assumption cannot be linked to a control, test, or monitoring signal, it remains an unsupported 
assumption rather than part of the assurance case. The following changes to a deployed system must trigger

--- page 85 ---
Page 85 
 
genai.owasp.org 
 
GenAI Security Project - Securing Agentic Applications V2 
 
explicit revalidation of affected scope elements (a partial replay of the affected design checks, red-team 
scenarios, and behavioral cases - not necessarily a full retest): 
• Any new tool integration or expansion of KC6 operational capabilities; 
• Any change to memory architecture (a KC4 type change); 
• Any modification to trust-boundary assignments for input sources; 
• Any update to system prompts or agent instructions; 
• Any change to orchestration logic or workflow transitions (KC2); 
• Any infrastructure change affecting environment assumptions; 
• Any incident or anomaly suggesting a declared mitigation did not operate as designed; 
• Background catalog drift: tools or skills appearing, disappearing, or being renamed in the MCP 
catalog without explicit human intervention; 
• Changes to third-party declarations relied upon by the assurance case (e.g., tool effect 
annotations, agent card claims, or skill manifest permissions), including declarations that have 
aged past their evidence window. 
Document the scoping decision and its rationale. An undocumented decision to skip revalidation is itself an 
assurance gap.

--- page 86 ---
Page 86 
 
genai.owasp.org 
 
GenAI Security Project - Securing Agentic Applications V2 
 
7.1 Red Teaming Agentic Applications 
Why agentic systems require red teaming. Three properties make them hard to validate by design-
time review alone. They are non-deterministic - the same input may not reliably produce the same 
output, so a passing test is one sample of possible behavior (one industry study ran a temperature-
zero prompt 1,000 times and saw 80 distinct completions). Agent behavior and effective capability 
emerge at runtime - tool use, memory, autonomy, external data, and accumulated state create 
execution paths that only appear in context. And agent failures have real-world consequences - 
when an agent can invoke tools, access data, or act with delegated privileges, a failure may be an 
unauthorized action, not merely a wrong answer. Red teaming should be integrated across the 
lifecycle (pre-deployment, on material change to model/prompt/tool surface/data 
access/permission boundary, and on a regular cadence between changes), not treated as a one-
time launch gate. For execution guidance - specific attack techniques, prompts, tools, and 
playbooks - refer to the OWASP ASI / CSA Agentic AI Red Teaming Guide and the OWASP GenAI Red 
Teaming Guide rather than this section. 
Red teaming simulates adversarial attacks to detect and address vulnerabilities in different scopes, starting 
with a specific application through the entire organization's security infrastructure. 
Red teaming strategy for agentic applications require complex interactions, autonomous decision-making, 
and integration with external systems. Proactive red teaming identifies possible attack vectors by assessing 
the key components of agentic systems, including not only prompt injection techniques, but also privilege 
escalation through tools, memory poisoning and plan manipulation. 
The OWASP ASI Red Teaming Guide for Agentic AI offers a risk-based methodology to handle security 
concerns with LLMs. It promotes a holistic approach that includes model review, implementation testing, 
infrastructure assessment, and runtime behavior analysis. Cross-functional coordination amongst data 
science, cybersecurity, ethical, and legal departments is critical. The guide encourages ongoing monitoring 
and iterative improvement in response to evolving AI threats. 
Prompt injection attacks and red teaming detection strategies: 
Prompt injection attacks target vulnerabilities in natural language processing systems by altering input to 
cause unauthorized actions. Such vulnerabilities might cause sensitive data leakage and bypass of defined 
guardrails. The use of red teaming tools can mimic multiple prompts to assess susceptibility to these 
attacks, utilizing technologies such as Promptfoo to automate the detection procedure. Continuous and 
proactive testing is required to anticipate new prompt injection tactics. 
OWASP ASI Red Teaming Guide listing available tools and datasets In Appendix B. 
Recently, new frameworks have started to be released and they are targeting agentic AI key components 
such as tool calling manipulation, privilege escalation and memory poisoning.

Privilege Escalation in Agentic Applications and Red Team Methodologies 
Privilege escalation attacks require acquiring illegal access to higher levels of control in a system. The ability 
of agentic AI to make independent decisions broadens the scope of potential attacks. Red teaming 
simulates situations to discover privilege escalation threats, such as leveraging inter-agent relationships 
and manipulating external integrations. Privilege escalation can affect widely, from the application itself, the 
deployed infrastructure, to affecting the agent's connected agencies, which allow it access to the external 
environment and additional systems. 
Memory Poisoning Threats and Red Teaming Techniques for Identification: 
Memory poisoning attacks can use either short-term memory, such as poisoned contextual information 
injected into the prompt, or through long-term memory and knowledge bases that introduce poisoned 
content that influence agent's decision-making. AgentPoison and ASB are red-teaming frameworks that 
employ memory poisoning attacks to discover such vulnerabilities, resulting in a high possibility of retrieving 
poisoned data.

--- page 89 ---
Page 89 
 
genai.owasp.org 
 
GenAI Security Project - Securing Agentic Applications V2 
 
7.2 Behavioral Testing for Agentic Applications 
Security framing. From a security perspective, behavioral testing measures whether the agent 
remains within its intended scope across representative in-scope usage, complementing the 
adversarial probing of the same boundary done by red teaming. It surfaces failures that require no 
attacker: 
1. Scope drift - gradual departure from the intended boundary on routine inputs; 
2. Silent composition - sequences of individually permitted actions that compose into an out-of-
scope outcome; 
3. Encoding gaps - declared constraints never correctly translated into operational controls; 
4. Over-restriction - blocking or escalation of legitimate in-scope requests. 
5. Control miscalibration — a binding guardrail, classifier, or policy control incorrectly permits out-
of-scope behavior or blocks legitimate in-scope behavior because of inaccurate or poorly 
calibrated decisions 
An agent that over-refuses has failed in its intended scope as surely as one that oversteps it. Persistent 
refusal may not be a sign of over-caution but an encoding failure or an inaccurate or miscalibrated control. 
Behavioral testing thereby makes the security–utility trade-off explicit and measurable. Its output is not a 
score but evidence: observed behavior categorized as in-scope, under-restrictive, or over-restrictive; each 
finding traceable to a stated design assumption, and, where possible, its root control failure. 
Behavioral testing for AI agents emphasizes evaluating their activities and interactions rather than solely 
examining their underlying structure or code. It is an essential assurance approach to ensure that agentic 
applications yield consistent and safe outcomes across diverse inputs and scenarios. 
This testing approach aims to uncover hidden problems such as unexpected actions, logical errors, or the 
pursuit of harmful goals. Behavioral testing methods require a systematic approach that encompasses 
defining explicit objectives for the agent, utilizing benchmark datasets to determine performance metrics, 
executing simulations in regulated environments to analyze the agent's behavior under varying conditions, 
and employing both human and automated assessments to evaluate the quality and safety of the results. 
• Benchmarks: Behavioral testing depends on recognized benchmark datasets and task suites as 
fundamental elements for standardizing performance evaluation. These benchmarks offer various 
tasks, datasets, and metrics intended to examine the capabilities and behaviors of AI agents in 
varied contexts and operational environments. 
Examples: 
o AgentBench: A comprehensive benchmark specifically designed to evaluate the task-
solving abilities of agents across various domains, including operating systems, databases, 
and knowledge graphs. It assesses planning, decision-making, and tool usage behaviors.

--- page 90 ---
Page 90 
 
genai.owasp.org 
 
GenAI Security Project - Securing Agentic Applications V2 
 
o HELM (Stanford): HELM evaluates models across multiple metrics including accuracy, 
robustness, fairness, bias, and toxicity, using standardized scenarios. Its results provide 
insights into model behaviors related to truthfulness and potential harms. 
o WebArena & The Agent Company: This benchmark evaluates autonomous agents 
performing tasks within realistic, complex web environments, testing behaviors like 
navigation, form filling, information retrieval, and adapting to dynamic website changes. 
• Evaluation Framework: A structured assessment framework offers a systematic process for 
implementing benchmarks and performing testing. These frameworks streamline the process of 
defining objectives, selecting test cases (often derived from benchmarks), executing tests in 
controlled or simulated environments, and analyzing results against expected behavioral standards 
(both positive and negative). 
Examples: 
o GenAI evaluation service (Google): Evaluation framework for any generative model or 
application and benchmark the evaluation results against defined judgment, using the 
user's evaluation criteria. 
o Bedrock Evaluations (Amazon): Evaluation framework for LLMs and integration with 
external sources as RAGs. 
Limits of general-purpose benchmarks. General-purpose benchmarks (AgentBench, HELM, 
WebArena, and similar) give a useful baseline for broad capabilities but are not designed to validate 
a deployed agentic system and should not serve as primary assurance evidence. Three limits apply: 
(1) generic context - they don't evaluate the deployment's specific capability set, trust boundaries, 
or operational environment, so a high-scoring agent may still over-refuse legitimate requests or 
under-refuse against its declared boundaries; (2) no capability composition - they evaluate 
capabilities in isolation, not as the deployed capability set, and don't model the lethal trifecta (2.7.3); 
(3) scores, not evidence - a score is not traceable to a declared design assumption and can't feed 
the verification queries below. Their appropriate use is pre-deployment sanity checks, regression 
detection after model/prompt changes, and a starting template for custom benchmarks (7.2.1). 
State these limits explicitly when reporting results. 
7.2.1 Custom Benchmark Construction 
A custom benchmark answers what a general-purpose one cannot: is this agent refusing requests it should 
permit? Permitting actions it should block? Does it behave correctly at the boundaries of its declared 
capability scope? 
a) Action-based construction. Start from the structured audit record (the behavioral tuple, 7.0.2): the 
tuple provides the observation structure, the benchmark provides the classification of whether an 
observed behavior was correct, incorrect, over-restrictive, or under-restrictive for this deployment.

--- page 91 ---
Page 91 
 
genai.owasp.org 
 
GenAI Security Project - Securing Agentic Applications V2 
 
1. Sample from the design-time scope (7.0.4) - generate test cases from the capability 
boundaries, trust-boundary declarations, and threat assumptions. Each case targets a specific 
declared boundary (a permitted capability, a prohibited one, an untrusted input source, a safe 
failure state). 
2. Classify expected tuples - for each case, define the expected action_taken and state_delta for 
correct behavior, and what they'd look like under over-/under-refusal. This is the benchmark 
specification. 
3. Execute and compare - run cases against the deployed agent, collect actual tuples, and 
compare field by field (not just the final output, but the reasoning step, policy context, and state 
delta). 
4. Classify failures by type - security failures (permitted something it should have blocked / 
under-refusal vs. declared boundaries), usability failures (blocked something it should have 
permitted / over-refusal vs. legitimate requests), and instrumentation failures (the tuple is 
incomplete - a coverage gap, not an agent-behavior problem). Both security and usability 
failures are assurance concerns; an over-refusal is often a signal that capability boundaries 
weren't correctly encoded into the operational controls. 
5. Integrate into CI/CD - a change to behavior-defining elements that shifts behavior relative to 
declared boundaries should block release the same way a failing security test does (see the 
revalidation triggers in 7.0.5). 
b) Trajectory-based construction. Classifying a single action tests instruction-following at one decision; it 
does not test whether the path stayed in scope. Two security-relevant properties are invisible at the 
single-action level: harness steering (the path is the joint product of model and harness, each 
conditioning the other) and composition (a sequence of individually permitted actions can compose into 
an out-of-scope outcome - the lethal trifecta is a property of a path, not any one action). A trajectory is 
the ordered sequence of steps (reasoning, tool selection, memory read/write, output) with each 
resulting state change and active policy context; a trajectory benchmark classifies whether that 
sequence stayed within the intended scope. The unit of evaluation is the path, not the endpoint. Four 
deviation types, each needing a different detection frame and response: 
Deviation type Where Trajectory signature Benchmark assertion Detection frame 
Honest 
misexecution 
In-session Path wanders off task, 
incoherent toward any 
goal, stalls or self-
corrects 
Trajectory 
completes the 
intended task 
without leaving 
scope 
Declared scope & 
task envelope

--- page 92 ---
Page 92 
 
genai.owasp.org 
 
GenAI Security Project - Securing Agentic Applications V2 
 
Overreach In-session Goal-directed sequence 
of individually permitted 
steps that incrementally 
extends capability, data 
access, or egress past 
the boundary
